newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: VISA APPLICANTS REJECTED ON GOOD CHARACTER REQUIREMENT
The World Jewish Congress says Australia's rejection of a visa application for controversial historian David Irving has no bearing on the question of free speech or censorship in this country.
The federal government rejected Mr Irving's and Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams' visa applications because both men failed to meet the good character requirement under the immigration act.
Congress chairman, Isi Leibler, says Mr Irving would have caused a lot of damage to Australia, at a time when inter-racial and ethnic relations are already inflamed.
He says Mr Irving's views are rubbish, and his association with radical right wing groups and neo Nazi's aren't welcome in Australia.
OPPOSITION BACKS VISA REJECTIONS
The Federal Opposition backs the Government's decision to refuse visas for controversial historian David irving and Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams to visit Australia.
Shadow Immigration Minister Duncan Kerr says to have allowed Mr Irving into Australia would have been divisive and painful for Holocaust survivors.
Mr Kerr says in view of the breakdown of the ceasefire in Northern Ireland and IRA hostilities, the Opposition understands the government's decision in relation to the Sinn Fein leader.
But he says in other circumstances an application from Mr Adams should perhaps be allowed to proceed as it has in other countries.
CAFE TO BE INCORPORATED INTO PORT ARTHUR MEMORIAL
The majority of surviving victims, local residents and doctors involved in the Port Arthur tradegy have agreed to the incorporation of the Broad Arrow Cafe as a memorial.
Part of the cafe, where 19 people were killed in the shootings, will be preserved.
This follows initial feelings that the building should be completely bulldozed.
Tasmanian Attorney General Ray Groom says 72 percent of submissions to the government wanted part to be incorporated into a memorial as a focus for rememberance and grieving.
Work on the memorial will start on the first anniversary of the shootings in April next year.
CONCERN FOR NURSES IN NT COMMUNITIES
Nurses working in remote Northern Territory communities are concerned about being exposed to potentially violent situations following the assault of a nurse on Tuesday night.
Police say the nurse was assaulted and had her ambulance stolenwhen she was driving a patient to an outstation.
The Australian Nursing Federation says four nurses have expressed concern about their safety in central Australian communities in the past seven weeks.
The Federation's John Haynes says if the complaints continue, the Federation will name those communities, and advise its members not to work in them.
RABBI LINKS PARLIAMENTARY PRIVILEGE WITH HOLOCAUST
At a memorial, marking the anniversary of the first day of the Holocaust in Nazi Germany, a New South Wales Rabbi has linked the Holocaust with the abuse of privilege in Australian parliaments.
Rabbi Brian Fox says the abuse of privilege by academics and politicians led to the Holocaust, and he's urged those with privilege to use it with care.
Representatives of all of the major religious denominations have gathered in Sydney's Martin Place to recall "Kristallnacht" -- the Night of Broken Glass.
On this night in 1938, 91 Jews were killed, 20-thousand arrested, and more then eight-thousand evicted from Berlin.
FIRST FEMALE BLACKHAWK PILOT LOOKING FORWARD TO CHALLENGE
The country's first fully qualified female Blackhawk pilot says she's looking forward to what will be a demanding job.
Twenty-six year old Lieutenant Ivana Gorlin has arrived in Townsville after completing 18 months of intensive officer and pilot training.
Lieutenant Gorlin, who says she wanted to fly Blackhawks after a helicopter flight while on holiday, says she's expecting a rewarding - if tough - job.
BAT CARERS TRY TO SAFEGUARD THEIR HEALTH

Members of a fruit bat carers network in central Queensland who've been bitten or scratched by flying foxes are being vaccinated today to help protect them against against a virus found in the animals.
The move comes as a Rockhampton woman is seriously ill after contracting the rare rabies-related Lyssavirus from a flying fox.
Queensland Health Minister Mike Horan says the virus is low risk as not many people handle sick bats, but those who do should be careful.
